title: Chrysippus the builder
hook: the third head of the school built its logic; without Chrysippus, the ancients said, no Stoa (Diogenes Laërtius 7.183)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cleanthes' hymn, the poem praising a reason that runs through all things. Your line was the one reason. Where did you find a thread of order? Day six hundred forty-three.

Every band has one. Every startup, every church committee, every family. Somebody had the vision, somebody had the heart, and then somebody came along and built the thing: wrote the rules, fixed the plumbing, made it last. Nobody puts that person on a poster. In the Stoic school, the visionary was Zeno, the heart was Cleanthes, and the builder was a long-distance runner from Asia Minor who wrote more books than anyone could count. The ancients had a saying about him. Today: Chrysippus the builder.
screen: `VISION, HEART, AND THE BUILDER.` → `NOBODY PUTS THE BUILDER ON A POSTER.` → `CHRYSIPPUS.`

segments.voice: First, the saying. Diogenes Laërtius reports it in his Lives: if there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa. The school would have faded, in other words, without him. He came from Soli, in what's now southern Turkey, and is said to have trained as a runner before turning to philosophy. He studied under Cleanthes, and became the third head of the school. Second, what he built. Chrysippus took Zeno's ideas, which had come under heavy attack from rival schools, and gave them structure: definitions, arguments, answers to objections. Above all, logic. He worked out a system for reasoning with whole statements: if this, then that; either this or that; not both. Modern logicians recognize it as an early form of what they call propositional logic. Third, his confidence. A story says he told Cleanthes: just teach me the doctrines, and I'll find the proofs myself. Diogenes says he wrote over seven hundred books. Every one of them is lost. Like Zeno, we know him through quotations, many of them from opponents arguing against him. Fourth, why a builder matters. Inspiration starts things. Structure keeps them alive. Epictetus and Marcus stood on what Chrysippus built, even when they never named him. The same is true of a good habit. A feeling gets you started. A small, steady structure, the same time, the same place, the same first step, is what gets you through the days you don't feel it.
screen: `NO CHRYSIPPUS, NO STOA.` · `IF THIS, THEN THAT: STOIC LOGIC.` · `SEVEN HUNDRED BOOKS, ALL LOST.` · `INSPIRATION STARTS; STRUCTURE LASTS.` · then, large: `THE BUILDER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you care about doing that keeps slipping: a walk, a call to your mother, this practice, reading. Now build one small structure for it, the way Chrysippus would, plain and logical. If this, then that. If I pour my coffee, then I sit for two minutes. If I park the car, then I call. Pick the trigger. Pick the step. Say the sentence to yourself once, clearly. The bell holds the time.
Chrysippus the builder. The third head of the Stoic school, who gave it structure and logic; without him, the ancients said, there'd be no Stoa. Today's word.
Your line: the builder. Today, run your if-this-then-that once, even if you don't feel like it. That's the structure doing its job. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Students of the Stoics know Chrysippus as the school's great systematizer, and historians of logic study his reconstructed system of reasoning with whole statements.

original.note: Greek: logic, the study of reasoning. For the Stoics, one of philosophy's three parts, with physics and ethics.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoicism came out finished from Zeno's head.
what it means: it took a builder, Chrysippus, to give the school structure and survive its critics.

what a scholar hears: Chrysippus's logic of propositions, with its basic argument forms, was largely reconstructed in the twentieth century from hostile sources, and recognized as a forerunner of modern propositional logic.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: 'If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa': DL 7.183. Paraphrased; confirm.
Born at Soli (Cilicia), long-distance runner before philosophy: DL 7.179. Confirm.
'Teach me the doctrines, I'll find the proofs': DL 7.179. Confirm.
Over 705 books: DL 7.180. Script says 'over seven hundred'; confirm.
Chrysippus as third scholarch after Cleanthes (from c. 230 BC). Confirm.
The Stoic logic reconstruction (e.g. Łukasiewicz 1935, Benson Mates 1953) is general knowledge; not cited by name in the voice.
